lessons.title: What Is System Design, for Data Engineers?

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a system you'd want in your own portfolio (it can preview the retail, warehouse-migration, or fraud-detector scenarios this chapter returns to later) and write a one-page requirements brief splitting it into a functional list (what it must do) and a non-functional list (freshness, scale, durability), the way this lesson modeled the split.
slots.deliverable: A one-page functional/non-functional requirements brief for a system of your choosing.

lessons.title: Choosing Storage — OLTP vs. OLAP vs. Object Storage

slots.practicalActivity: Run a back-of-the-envelope estimation for your chosen system (events/sec, storage/year, read QPS), then use the OLTP-vs-OLAP-vs-object-storage framework to pick one storage option and justify it in writing against your own numbers.
slots.deliverable: A back-of-envelope calculation sheet plus a one-paragraph storage-choice justification.

lessons.title: Choosing a Processing Model — Batch, Streaming, or Hybrid

slots.practicalActivity: Decide whether your system needs batch, streaming, or hybrid processing, then sketch a Lambda architecture diagram for it (speed layer, batch layer, serving layer) covering the case where the two layers genuinely need different logic.
slots.deliverable: A labeled Lambda architecture diagram (boxes and arrows) for your system.

lessons.title: Data Modeling at Scale — Star Schema Revisited

slots.practicalActivity: Redraw your system as Kappa architecture and write 3-4 sentences on which one — Lambda or Kappa — actually fits it better and why. Then fix your system's fact grain in one sentence before sketching its star schema (one fact table plus at least two dimensions).
slots.deliverable: A Lambda-vs-Kappa decision note plus a star schema sketch with the grain stated explicitly.

slots.practicalActivity: Choose a partitioning key for your system's main fact table and justify it against at least one real query pattern it has to serve fast. Then decide whether the system needs sharding, and if so, pick a shard key and write what breaks if that key choice were wrong.
slots.deliverable: A partitioning-and-sharding decision writeup for your system's main data store.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify one step in your system where the same event could be processed twice, and design an idempotent key for it (a MERGE-on-event-id pattern). Then state in writing whether your system needs exactly-once delivery or can safely tolerate at-least-once, and why.
slots.deliverable: An idempotency-and-delivery-guarantee design note with one concrete MERGE/upsert key.

slots.practicalActivity: Design the ingestion layer for your system (sources, landing format, a raw bronze-style zone) and the transformation layer that follows it (bronze to silver to gold), citing the medallion pattern from the Databricks & Delta Lake course.
slots.deliverable: An ingestion-and-transformation layer design diagram with each layer's responsibility labeled.

slots.practicalActivity: Design the serving layer for your system's dashboard — name the query engine and the latency it must hit — then decide what, if anything, needs caching to actually hit that latency, and justify the decision.
slots.deliverable: A serving-layer design note stating the latency target and the caching decision.

slots.practicalActivity: Decide whether your system needs multi-tenant isolation (separate workspaces or row-level security) and write it down either way, then turn your system's freshness requirement into an actual number (for example 'under 15 minutes') instead of a vague word like 'real-time.'
slots.deliverable: A multi-tenancy decision plus a numeric freshness SLA for your system.

lessons.title: Trade-off Analysis — CAP Theorem for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: For your own system, write out which two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance you'd sacrifice under a network partition, and defend that choice in 4-5 sentences the way you'd defend it out loud in a design interview.
slots.deliverable: A one-page CAP theorem trade-off defense for your system.

lessons.title: Case Study: A Ride-Sharing Analytics Platform
Case Study: A Real-Time Fraud Detection System

slots.practicalActivity: Whiteboard the ride-sharing analytics platform and the real-time fraud detection system from memory, before reviewing each case study's own architecture, then compare your sketches against the lesson's and note exactly what you missed.
slots.deliverable: Two from-memory architecture sketches with a written gap-analysis against each case study.

lessons.title: Case Study: A Retail Inventory Data Platform
Case Study: A Social Media Analytics Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Whiteboard the retail inventory platform and the social media analytics pipeline from memory, the same way as last session, then compare against each lesson's real design and note what you missed this time.
slots.deliverable: Two more from-memory architecture sketches with written gap notes.

lessons.title: Presenting a System Design — Whiteboarding Like an Interview

slots.practicalActivity: Record yourself (phone video or audio) presenting your own system's design end-to-end in under 5 minutes — requirements, estimation, storage, processing, serving — using this lesson's whiteboarding structure. Then write a half-page recap of the chapter's 25 lessons in your own words.
slots.deliverable: A self-recorded 5-minute design presentation plus a personal chapter-recap summary.

slots.practicalActivity: Look up the current DP-700 exam skills-measured page and copy its domain weightings into a tracking sheet you'll update after every practice-question lesson in this chapter.
slots.deliverable: A DP-700 domain-weighting tracker spreadsheet, started.

lessons.title: Implementing and Managing an Analytics Solution
Ingesting and Transforming Data — Exam Focus

slots.practicalActivity: Using the Fabric & Real-Time Analytics material, write out the exact steps you'd take to implement an analytics solution and the exact steps to ingest and transform data in Fabric, matching each step to the exam domain it falls under on your tracker.
slots.deliverable: Two step-by-step exam-domain checklists added to your tracker.

lessons.title: Monitoring and Optimizing a Solution — Exam Focus

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the monitoring-and-optimizing checklist for a Fabric solution (capacity metrics, pipeline monitoring, query performance) and tag each item with the exam domain it belongs to.
slots.deliverable: A monitoring/optimizing checklist tagged by exam domain.

slots.practicalActivity: Work the practice question sets on OneLake/Lakehouses, Data Warehouses, and Eventstreams/KQL under a 2-minute-per-question timer each, score yourself immediately after each set, and log every miss in your domain tracker.
slots.deliverable: Three scored practice sets logged in your domain tracker.

slots.practicalActivity: Work the practice sets on Notebooks/Spark, Security/Governance, and Monitoring/Deployment the same timed way, and update your domain tracker's running miss-count per domain.
slots.deliverable: Three more scored practice sets with an updated domain miss-count.

slots.practicalActivity: Read through the common DP-700 traps and flag any you've already fallen for in your practice sets. Then build your real personalized study plan (which domains need another pass, in what order) and a written exam-day timing strategy (minutes per question, flag-and-skip rule).
slots.deliverable: A personalized DP-700 study plan plus a written exam-day timing strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the full nine-question Part 1 practice exam under an 18-20 minute timer exactly as instructed, without checking any answer mid-set, then score it afterward and sort your misses by domain into your tracker.
slots.deliverable: A scored Part 1 practice exam with misses sorted by domain.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the Part 2 practice exam under the same timed conditions, score it, then write a half-page recap: which domain needed the most review across both exams, and what you're changing in your study plan as a result.
slots.deliverable: A scored Part 2 practice exam plus a written DP-700 chapter-recap note.

lessons.title: Why AI Matters for Data Engineers Now

slots.practicalActivity: Open Copilot inside a Fabric notebook (or read its documentation closely if you don't have a live workspace handy) and list three concrete data-engineering tasks it could realistically speed up for your own work.
slots.deliverable: A three-item list of Copilot-in-Fabric use cases relevant to your own work.

lessons.title: Using Copilot to Generate a Notebook

slots.practicalActivity: Write a Copilot-style prompt asking it to generate a PySpark cell for a real transformation (for example a dedup-plus-SCD-Type-2 merge from the Databricks & Delta Lake course), then manually review the generated code line by line as if Copilot had actually produced it, flagging anything you wouldn't trust without checking.
slots.deliverable: A prompt-and-generated-code review writeup with at least two flagged review points.

lessons.title: Using Copilot to Explain and Fix a KQL Query

slots.practicalActivity: Write a KQL query with a deliberate bug (a wrong summarize window, say), draft the Copilot-style prompt you'd use to get it explained and fixed, then verify the suggested fix by hand against KQL syntax rules rather than trusting it blindly.
slots.deliverable: A broken KQL query, a Copilot-style fix prompt, and the corrected query with your own verification notes.

lessons.title: AI-Assisted Data Quality — Anomaly Detection Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one of your pipeline's real tables and write the anomaly-detection rules you'd want flagged (a null spike, a volume drop, an out-of-range value), then draft an LLM prompt that would generate documentation for that table's schema.
slots.deliverable: An anomaly-detection rule list plus a draft LLM documentation prompt for one table.

lessons.title: Prompting Patterns for Data Engineering Tasks

slots.practicalActivity: Write three of your own original prompting patterns for data-engineering tasks, then explain the four RAG stages (index-time embed, query-time embed, retrieve, generate) in your own words using one of your own tables as the worked example.
slots.deliverable: Three original data-engineering prompts plus a RAG-stages explanation using your own data.

lessons.title: Building a Vector Index Over Your Data Catalog
A RAG Pipeline Over Fabric Metadata

slots.practicalActivity: Build a toy RAG pipeline by hand: write short text chunks describing 4-5 of your own tables (name, description, columns), 'embed' them by writing keyword tags, then trace a real question ('which table has X data?') through the retrieve and generate steps the way the lesson traced its own churn-data example — and make the generated answer name its source table.
slots.deliverable: A hand-built mini RAG trace (chunks, a test question, the retrieved chunk, and a cited generated answer) over your own catalog.

lessons.title: Using an LLM to Draft a Root Cause Analysis

slots.practicalActivity: Draft AI-style test cases for one of your own pipeline's transformations (nulls, duplicates, late-arriving data), then write a draft AI-assisted root-cause-analysis note for a hypothetical pipeline failure, citing which log or metric would actually confirm your hypothesis.
slots.deliverable: A test-case list and a draft root-cause-analysis note for one pipeline scenario.

lessons.title: Guardrails — What Not to Hand an LLM

slots.practicalActivity: Map two legacy-style source schemas to one target schema the way an AI-assisted mapping tool would suggest, then write your own guardrails checklist: what you would never hand an LLM from your own data (PII columns, credentials, secrets).
slots.deliverable: A schema-mapping table plus a personal AI-guardrails checklist.

lessons.title: Cost and Latency Trade-offs of AI-Augmented Pipelines
A Worked Example: AI-Assisted Pipeline Debugging

slots.practicalActivity: Estimate the cost-and-latency cost of adding one AI call to a real pipeline step, write your own evaluation checklist for judging whether that AI's output is actually correct, then work through the AI-assisted-debugging example and reproduce its diagnosis in your own words.
slots.deliverable: A cost/latency estimate, an evaluation checklist, and your own written walkthrough of the worked debugging example.

lessons.title: Where AI Fits in the Production Practices From Course 3
The Limits of AI in Data Engineering, Honestly
AI for Data Engineers Chapter Recap

slots.practicalActivity: Write a half-page note on where AI fits into the production practices from the Databricks & Delta Lake course, an equally honest half-page on where AI's limits would bite your own capstone projects, and a closing recap of this chapter in your own words.
slots.deliverable: A three-part reflection note closing out the AI chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Read the three project briefs ahead (a real-time retail analytics platform, a multi-source warehouse migration, a streaming fraud detector) and set up a project folder or repo for each one with a placeholder README, so all three builds have a home before Project 1 starts.
slots.deliverable: Three project folders/repos, one per capstone, each with a placeholder README.

lessons.title: Project 1 Kickoff: A Real-Time Retail Analytics Platform

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 1's full functional/non-functional requirements list from the brief given, fix the fact grain at one row per line item per sale, and write the batch-vs-streaming-vs-hybrid ingestion decision with your own justification, exactly as the lesson modeled it.
slots.deliverable: Project 1's requirements doc, grain statement, and ingestion-model decision, saved into its project folder.

slots.practicalActivity: Design Project 1's ingestion layer in full: sketch the bronze landing paths for nightly POS exports and the Eventstream-fed online orders, write the idempotent MERGE-on-event-id SQL pattern for the online path, and state the real freshness SLA (minutes for online, next-morning for in-store).
slots.deliverable: Project 1's ingestion design doc with a landing-zone diagram and a working idempotent MERGE statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Build out Project 1's transformation layer: write the silver-layer cleaning rules and the gold-layer aggregation query that rolls sales up by region and category at the grain fixed at kickoff.
slots.deliverable: Project 1's silver cleaning logic and a gold-layer SQL aggregation query, committed to the project repo.

slots.practicalActivity: Design Project 1's serving layer and sketch the actual dashboard — sales by region and category, refreshed on the SLA you set — wireframing it or building it in a BI tool if one is available to you.
slots.deliverable: A serving-layer design note plus a dashboard wireframe or working dashboard for Project 1.

slots.practicalActivity: Harden Project 1 for production: write the error-handling plan for a failed batch load, the monitoring metrics you'd alert on, and what happens to the dashboard if the Eventstream goes down for an hour.
slots.deliverable: A production-hardening checklist (errors, monitoring, alerting) for Project 1.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 1's honest retrospective: what you built, which named techniques it used, and what would break first at 10x traffic — the exact structure the lesson's wrap-up asks for.
slots.deliverable: Project 1's written retrospective, saved as the start of its README's 'hard decisions' section.

lessons.title: Project 2 Kickoff: A Multi-Source Data Warehouse Migration

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 2's requirements for consolidating three legacy sources into one Fabric Data Warehouse, and justify warehouse-over-lakehouse in your own words for this specific cross-source BI-reporting use case.
slots.deliverable: Project 2's requirements doc and storage-choice justification.

lessons.title: Project 2: Source Assessment and Migration Plan

slots.practicalActivity: Assess Project 2's three legacy sources for key mismatches (no shared customer/product key scheme yet) and write a migration-order plan — which source moves first and why — plus the reconciliation check you'd run to confirm totals match during the coexistence period.
slots.deliverable: Project 2's source-assessment notes and a migration-order-and-reconciliation plan.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the target Fabric Data Warehouse schema for Project 2: write the DDL (or a schema diagram) for the consolidated fact and dimension tables that unify orders, customers, and inventory.
slots.deliverable: Project 2's target warehouse schema (DDL or diagram), committed to the project repo.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 2's phased cutover plan: the order systems go live in, the minimal scheduled downtime window, and the rollback contingency if reconciliation fails partway through a phase.
slots.deliverable: Project 2's written cutover strategy with a rollback contingency.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 2's honest retrospective, the same structure as Project 1's: what was built, which named techniques it used, and what you'd change at 10x scale or with a fourth legacy source added.
slots.deliverable: Project 2's written retrospective.

lessons.title: Project 3 Kickoff: An End-to-End Streaming Fraud Detector

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 3's requirements table (throughput, latency, delivery, idempotency) and run the back-of-envelope numbers — transactions/sec, p99 latency budget, retention days — that rule out a batch design before any architecture gets drawn.
slots.deliverable: Project 3's requirements table and back-of-envelope sizing numbers.

lessons.title: Project 3: Streaming Ingestion and Feature Computation

slots.practicalActivity: Design Project 3's streaming ingestion path: sketch Event Hub to Eventstream to feature-computation, and write the windowed aggregation logic (sliding vs. tumbling, and why) for computing fraud features in real time.
slots.deliverable: Project 3's ingestion-and-feature-computation design with a stated windowing choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Design Project 3's scoring-and-alerting step: state what the serving layer must guarantee to hit the sub-second latency budget under peak load, and write the alert rule that fires when a transaction gets flagged.
slots.deliverable: Project 3's scoring-and-alerting design note with the latency guarantee stated explicitly.

slots.practicalActivity: Write Project 3's honest retrospective: the watermark/window trade-off you'd defend in an interview, and what you'd do differently now, knowing what you know.
slots.deliverable: Project 3's written retrospective.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the README for all three capstone projects following the four-question structure (what it does, what it looks like, what were the hard decisions, how do I run it), pulling the 'hard decisions' section straight from each project's own retrospective, and sketch one five-or-six-box architecture diagram per project.
slots.deliverable: Three complete project READMEs with architecture diagrams, assembled into one portfolio.

lessons.title: Telling Your Project Story in an Interview

slots.practicalActivity: For each of the three projects, write out the Situation -> Design -> Trade-off -> Retrospect script, then rehearse saying each one out loud, unscripted, in under two minutes, at least twice per project.
slots.deliverable: Three written interview narratives (one per project) that you've rehearsed out loud.

lessons.title: Data Engineering Career & Capstone — Course and Track Finale

slots.practicalActivity: Write a half-page reflection on the whole four-course Data Engineering track: which skill from each course your three capstones actually used, and what you'd build next with them.
slots.deliverable: A closing reflection note on the full Data Engineering track, filed alongside your capstone portfolio.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: By finishing this course, a student can design a system the way a working data engineer does, speak DP-700 exam material fluently enough to sit the certification, use AI tools responsibly inside a Fabric pipeline, and point to three fully built, retrospected capstone projects with real READMEs and rehearsed interview narratives — completing the entire Azure/Fabric Data Engineer path.
